beats.intro: Lesson fourteen. [[sub]]When one team becomes many: what to decide centrally, and what to leave local.
beats.success: Part three of the book picks up the breakfast factory where we left it. [[egg]]Business was so good that we bought a continuous egg-boiling machine. It was expensive, [[uni]]but breakfasts came out more uniform than ever. [[full]]Volume grew until the machine ran at full capacity, [[cost]]so the cost of each breakfast kept falling. [[pass]]We passed some of the savings on to customers, and our reputation spread.
beats.grow: So we did what entrepreneurs do. [[two]]We opened a second Breakfast Factory across town, and it worked too. [[mag]]Then a national magazine, Neighborhood Gourmet, ran a story on us. [[fran]]We seized the moment and franchised nationwide, moving into neighborhoods with the right mix of customers. [[net]]Soon we were running a vast network, more than a hundred restaurants. [[diff]]And the network needed very different tasks and skills from running one restaurant.
beats.tension: The most important new task is a balance. [[local]]On one side, a local entrepreneur runs each franchise. He knows his neighborhood, so he can adapt to it and, we hope, run the most profitable restaurant possible. [[scale]]On the other side, with over a hundred restaurants, our purchasing power is immense. Done centrally, many things get done better and much cheaper than any one branch could manage. [[qual]]And above all, quality is the real secret of our business. No branch, and no region, can be allowed to put it at risk. [[theme]]Grove calls this the dichotomy between centralization and decentralization, and it runs through everything the network does.
beats.local: So, item by item, where should each decision sit? [[ad]]Advertising, local or national? The local manager probably knows who reads the Daily Blatt, his neighborhood paper. Headquarters does not. [[hire]]Hiring and firing, and wage scales? Labor markets differ from region to region, so one national pay scale hardly makes sense. [[mach]]But the sophisticated automatic machinery is bought centrally. It took a long time to find suitable vendors, and to learn to test incoming machines against our demanding requirements. [[chi]]A sizable group in Chicago does only that. No branch or region should duplicate it.
beats.middle: Some things belong in between. [[eggs]]Eggs, for instance. Not all bought in Chicago: they must be fresh, and nobody wants to truck such a delicate cargo all over the country. [[insp]]Yet we don't want every branch running its own egg inspection either. [[reg]]The compromise is regional egg purchasing centers, each a few hours by truck from every branch in its region. [[std]]Quality standards, though, are national: uniform and high everywhere, and we monitor every franchise against them. [[menu]]The menu is split. A core menu everywhere, so customers can count on the basics, [[taste]]with some room for regional tastes.
beats.q2: Quick check. Local, regional or central?
beats.more: The questions keep coming. [[re]]Real estate: any local building, or one uniform design built from the ground up? Perhaps any available building, as long as it meets standards set in Chicago. [[furn]]Furniture: must it be identical? Should Chicago buy it all? [[table]]Tableware: people link what they eat from with the breakfast itself, so it should be the same everywhere, and might as well be bought in one place. [[plates]]But it is silly for a branch in Montana to ask Chicago for a few broken plates. So, a couple of regional warehouses. [[site]]And where should a new franchise go in a city? Chicago? The chief executive? The local manager? [[ask]]Or perhaps Chicago, after consulting the regional managers, who know their areas better.
beats.overhead: Things have become very complicated. [[wish]]Behind his big desk at headquarters, the chief executive wishes he were back pouring the coffee himself, [[one]]or at least running one restaurant, where he knew everybody by name and made every decision without a mountain of pros and cons. [[none]]Back then there was almost no overhead. [[now]]Now there is a corporate personnel manager. [[traffic]]A traffic manager wants a computer to route eggs from the regional centers. He promises lower trucking costs, same-day delivery, and the smallest possible stock of tableware. [[estate]]Soon there will be a real estate manager too. [[point]]Coordinating many teams is real work, and it creates jobs of its own.
beats.teams: Earlier we said management is a team game: [[out]]a manager's output is the output of the organizations under her supervision or influence. [[tot]]Now we find it is more than that. A manager has to build a team of teams, [[fit]]where each team sits in a suitable and mutually supportive relationship with the others. [[next]]The next lessons show how: hybrid organizations, dual reporting, and the modes of control.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Growth turns one team into a network of teams. [[w2]]Every network weighs local knowledge against economies of scale. [[w3]]Leave local what local knowledge improves, like hiring, pay and local advertising. [[w4]]Centralize what needs scale, scarce skills, or one shared standard of quality. [[w5]]Use a regional middle when both matter, and build a team of teams. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson fourteen.
